_note: Newest first. The top version must match MARKETING_VERSION in project.yml (tools/check_content.py checks). 1.0.0 is the App Store release.

releases.title: Bosses with a story
notes: Boss fights happen right where you stand, with the map behind them like any battle, and a boss brings two of the area's own monsters along, a little weaker than itself, standing at its sides.

The first time you beat a boss, a short story tells what the win means: who's free again, which road opens, who'll want to hear about it, and where the trail leads next. Bosses you've beaten keep their story in the Monster Book, so you can read the ones you won before this update too.
The Earth Snake is brown all over now, without the green that showed through on its coils, and the Light Snake is the pale, glassy gold its description promises instead of salmon and olive.

Your companion takes orders, like in Fairyland Online: after you choose your own move, choose its: Attack, one of its skills, Guard, or Auto to let it decide. It gets its own 5 seconds, and fights on its own when they run out. Rather it fought alone? Turn off "Choose your companion's moves" in Settings.

Curses and poison, Fairyland's dark arts: a poisoned fighter loses HP at the end of every round for 3 rounds, and a cursed one hits 20% weaker for 3 rounds. A green drop or a violet arrow by the HP bar shows the rounds left. Mages learn Curse at level 12 and Poison at 25. Watch out for the Venom Bite of snakes and widows, the Poison Skeleton's Poison Mist, and the Evil Eye of phantoms and Idreus.

Bigger parties: up to four friends can travel with you now, a party of five, and they bring their companions. Each companion walks at its friend's side, fights beside them, and shows next to them in the Companions list. In battle a party of more than five stands with the people in front and the companions in a row behind. A friend who's around while your party is full says so instead of showing nothing.

releases.title: Spells that land
notes: Stone Spike bursts out of the ground in real rock: the earth cracks, shaded spikes shoot up round the target (tall ones behind, short ones in front), throwing rocks and dust and knocking it off its feet, then sink back. The more you train it, the more spikes, up to a giant one at the top.

Fire Bolt is a flickering fireball trailing embers that bursts into a blast, burns out into smoke and scorches the ground. Stronger casts set flames licking round the target and send a column of fire up through it.
Leaf Storm whips leaves, and petals as it grows, into a cyclone round every foe, passing in front of them and behind with gusts of wind.
Monsters' water spells (Bubble, Jelly Splash, Frost Breath) lob a wobbling orb of water that bursts in a splash and a spray of drops.
Mastered spells finish with the new art too: a rain of fireball meteors, a forest of stone spikes, a hurricane of leaves.

With three or more of you travelling together, the faces in the top left fold into one row of small faces under yours (your companion's with its HP), so they no longer cover the map. Tap the row to see everyone in full, and the arrow to fold it again.
Beat another adventurer in a duel, or one who picks a fight with you, and they drop everything they carry: the goods they'd have sold you that day go into your bag.
While you talk to someone (or trade, chat or open a menu), the joystick and the buttons step aside instead of peeking out from behind the conversation.

Your companion and friends no longer walk through water or cave walls: where there's no room beside you, they fall in behind you in single file, in your footsteps. Adventurers' pets keep to dry land too.
Caves are dark now: you see as far as your light reaches, a warm circle round you that flickers like a flame, and beyond it the dark. Glowing crystals and moss still shine faintly through it.
In a cave the minimap shows only what your light has fallen on, so you map it as you go instead of seeing every passage from the start. What you've explored is saved.

Battles keep moving: you have 5 seconds to choose each turn, counting down in a bar under the battle log. When it runs out you attack, going for the monster you last hit (or the first one standing). The clock waits while the chat is open or you're moving the buttons around.

releases.title: Hair that fits
notes: Each gender keeps its own hair: a female human's ponytail, an Other human's bob, a male elf's swept hair, an Other elf's shoulder-length hair, a female dwarf's braids and an Other dwarf's messy mop are the styles they start with, and theirs alone. Picking another style no longer leaves the old locks and braids hanging.

Every hairstyle sits right on every head: an elf's ears poke through instead of stretching into wings, no stray ear tips or collar bits ride along, and a style takes your race's own hair colour (blonde on an elf) until you dye it.
Dyeing your hair no longer dyes your boots, belt and cuffs.

Tap an item when trading, in a shop or at the smith to see all about it: who can use it and from what level, its stats against what you're wearing, and what a material forges into. Gear you couldn't use says why right in the list (Beast Tamers only, Needs level 30).

releases.title: Every hair
notes: Dyeing your hair now colours all of it. The darker and redder strands at the edges kept their ginger before, and so did much of an elf's long hair; now every shade takes the new colour.
Hair that falls over the shoulders, side locks and beards (a female dwarf's long hair, a male elf's beard) take the colour too.
Changing your gear: Unequip now sits beside the item you're wearing, Done closes the list from below it, and the items to choose from line up with the one you're wearing.
Skills on the Character screen show their MP after the name, like Bash (12 MP), with the mastery bar at the right end of the row.
The coins next to your gold on the calendar plate are easy to see: a deeper gold with a dark edge, as big as the sun and moon.
In battle every ground circle is seen from the same angle (heroes stood on flatter circles than monsters), and both sides line up at the same slope however many fight on each side.

Levelling up is a big moment now: light pours down on your hero and LEVEL UP! fills the battlefield with the jingle, then the victory card (and the quest card) shows your new level on a gold medal with the stats it raised.

releases.title: Rare finds
notes: Six rare monsters that never turned up now do: the Azure Golden Hamster and Starry Hedgehog on the Northern Grassland, the Rosy Wood Crab and Frosted Mud Eagle on Pineapple Shore, the Crimson Yellow Butterfly in Lotus Land and the Amber Werewolf in Big Bad Wolf's Lair. The Monster Book can be filled at last.
A companion or friend who goes on guard in battle really does take half damage for the rest of the round, like you do.
The Companions page gives the real capture rule: weaken the last wild monster standing to 20% HP or less (it used to say half).

releases.title: Face forward
notes: Female humans, male elves and female dwarves (and the other body type) showed the back of their head in the round portrait top-left and in other pictures facing you. They face you now.
While you wear armour, Customize leaves out the Outfit section entirely instead of explaining why it can't be changed.
In battle the monsters and your party stand further apart, so the two sides read as lines facing off instead of a crowd.
The items you find after a battle (or get from a quest) sit centred on the card.
The Monster Book no longer says Light and Dark monsters are both strong against and weak to each other: it says they hit each other extra hard.
You can chat during a fight: the Chat button sits under the battle log on the right.
The world map opens centred on where you are, instead of on the middle of the map with your town cut off at the edge.

Mastered skills (yours, your party's and bosses') put on a real show: the battlefield dims, a magic circle and a pillar of light rise under the caster, and the skill ends in a finale in its own element: a meteor rain, a tidal wave, a forest of stone spikes, a leaf hurricane, pillars of holy light, a tornado or giant crossing blades.

Everyone fights in their own style. Fighters close in with a double slash, mages stay back and fire a bolt of magic from a rune circle, beast tamers pounce with claw marks. Before a skill, a mage draws a rune circle, a fighter flares up in a battle aura and a tamer calls a swirl of wild spirits. Elves dart in quicker and shed leaves, dwarves hit hard enough to shake the ground.
A friend in your party brings their companion into battle too.
Skill names in battle no longer show the skill's level (Lv 7): just the name.

releases.title: Dressed for battle
notes: While you wear armour, Customize no longer offers outfit colours: the armour decides how your clothes look. Take it off to dye your clothes again.
Levelling up no longer opens the skill card when every skill you know is mastered and there's nothing new to learn; points are kept for the next skill your class unlocks.
Shops buy too: tap Sell in any shop to sell materials and gear you've outgrown for half their price.
Trade with adventurers you meet: tap Trade on their card. They pay half again what a shop would for things they want, and sell a few things of their own. Offers change every in-game day.

Skills take 10 steps to master instead of 5, each step a little stronger (a mastered skill still hits 80% harder than a new one). Your progress carries over: a skill at level 3 is now level 6, and mastered skills stay mastered.
Skill levels show as a ten-segment gauge that warms from bronze to silver to gold, and shimmers in rainbow colours once mastered.
Battles face off across the screen's diagonal: monsters up on the left looking down at you, your party lower on the right looking back up at them, both lines centred.
The victory card shows EXP with a star and gold with coins, and what you found as little item pictures with counts, instead of a list of lines.
In battle every fighter with MP shows a blue MP bar under their HP bar, and pinned skill buttons are labelled with the skill's name (cut short with … if it's long) instead of its MP cost.
The world map is turned like the game's view, with a compass: north is up-left and east is up-right, so the road you take off the top-right of the screen leads to the place up-right on the map.
Bars use the same colours everywhere: HP red, MP blue, EXP green. Battle HP bars were green, and your companion's HP bar on the map was orange.

Handing in a quest opens a Quest complete card like the victory card after a battle: EXP with a star, gold with coins, items as little pictures, plus any new looks and roads it opens. If it levels you up, the skill card follows.

New Monster Book (Companions → Monster Book): every monster you meet in battle is written down, with its lore, element (and what it's strong against and weak to), stats at the level you met it, skills, where it lives, rare drops and how many you've beaten. Monsters you haven't met yet show as dark silhouettes; filter the book by element.
Monsters of the same kind in one battle are just called by their name, without the A, B, C after it.

releases.title: Clean corner
notes: The four menu buttons on the map (Character, Companions, Bag, Quests) are icons only now, without the text underneath.
The title screen card is tidier: the hero's name and the companion line are gone (Continue already says who you are), leaving the hero and companion with your class, level and map.

releases.title: Light and strings
notes: New spells in the spirit of Fairyland's Acolyte of Light. Mages learn Recovery (Lv 10, heal an ally), Bridge of Light (Lv 20), Revive (Lv 35, wake a fainted ally mid-battle) and Bless (Lv 45, +25% strength and defense for 3 turns, more at higher levels). Tamers learn Revive at Lv 30, to bring a fainted companion back.
Bridge of Light is cast from the Character screen outside battle: tap Cast to be carried back to your last checkpoint.
The party heal Blessing is now called Healing Spring, like the original spell.
Wooden Puppets and the Puppet King look like real marionettes now, strings and all, instead of recoloured skeletons.
Tapping the minimap opens the world map only. The full map of the area you're in no longer shows, so caves and forests stay a mystery until you explore them.

releases.title: Signs and smiles
notes: Roads out of a map have a wooden signpost again. Walk up to it (a ? shows when you're close) and tap it to read where the road goes; tapping from afar walks you over first.
The title screen shows your hero facing you and breathing like they do in the game, with your companion close beside them doing its own idle bounce or sway.
The loading bar matches its percentage, and it learns how long each part of a map takes on your phone, so it fills at the real pace from the second visit on.
Hits in battle burst into a small fireball (hot core, flames, embers and a puff of smoke) instead of a cartoon star; critical hits blaze bigger, splash hits smaller, and heals glow green.

releases.title: Watch it fill
notes: Loading screens show a blue bar with a percentage instead of a spinner. The map is built a piece at a time behind it, so the bar moves as the ground, scenery, buildings and people go up.
In battle, names are smaller and sit right on top of each fighter's HP bar, so the field isn't covered in big labels.
Tap a quest in the Quests list to see its reward: gold, EXP, items with their icons, new looks and roads it opens. Tap a completed quest to see what it said and what you earned.
The title screen shows your active companion walking beside your hero.

releases.title: Tidy buttons
notes: Battle buttons sit in neat rows beside the big button instead of a tall column over your party, with More on top of the big button.
Pinned skills are round like the other battle buttons, with their MP cost underneath.

Rearranging works like the iPhone home screen: hold any battle button and they all wiggle. Drag one over another to take its place, onto the big button to make it the big one, or into the "Behind More" tray. Tap Done when you're happy.

releases.title: Back on the road
notes: Fixed: the game could crash while loading a map. Drawing the minimap's colours took so long on big maps that iOS stopped the app.
Deleting a game moved off the title screen, where its little × looked like it only closed the notice. It's now under Settings → Danger zone inside the game, and asks before deleting.

releases.title: Quieter streets
notes: Names step aside: your hero's and companions' names hide while you walk and come back when you stop.
Everyone else's name shows only when you walk up to them or tap them.
Arrange your battle buttons: hold any of them, then drag them into the order you like. The top one becomes the big button, so Attack can make way for a skill, and anything can go behind More.

releases.title: Glory in numbers
notes: Bigger battles: monster groups grow as you travel, from one to three in the first fields to as many as ten in the far lands, lined up in two rows.

Upgraded skills feel it: from level 2 your hero gathers power first, at 3 and 4 the hit bursts with rings, light rays and falling sparkles, and a mastered skill (level 5) blazes in gold with its name across the screen.
Class skills are spread over the long climb: new ones open at levels 15 to 70 instead of all before 30.
Play several heroes: a new game gets its own save, and the title screen lets you swipe between your games (and delete old ones).
The title screen shows each hero as they look in the game: race, hairstyle, colours and armour.
The quest list shows who gave you each quest, with their face and where they live, so you know where to report back.
Your hero walks on the Character screen and the title screen, turning to show every side.

releases.title: Within reach
notes: Battle buttons sit in one column right beside Attack: More at the bottom, Skills above it, and Capture, Items and your pinned skills stacking on top.
Your hero's name and gender are set for good when you create them; Customize still changes hairstyle and colours.
The minimap takes its colours from the map itself, so a purple wood or a snowy field looks the part.
Fixed light corners around the edge of the screen on moody maps like Twilight Woods.

releases.title: Into the mist
notes: Fixed a crash when continuing a game saved before 0.2.0 with friends in it.
The land beyond each map's edge now fades into a soft mist (a deep gloom in caves) instead of black.
A companion that faints stays down after the battle: it sits out fights and stops following you until a potion or a healer wakes it up, and earns no EXP from that fight.
Fixed the intro's first page running off the screen.

releases.title: A bigger Fairyland
notes: The world grows to 30 maps, with a world atlas, winding roads, caves, snowfall, icy ponds and busier towns.
Levels now run to 105 and beyond, and you join a guild at level 10.
Three new bosses: Grumpy Old Oak, Great Wisp and the Moon Rabbit Queen. Bosses can be fought again, and six of them may drop a rare colour of their armour.
Choose male, female or other and a hairstyle. Helmets and hoods now cover your hair, and stronger armour shows finer detail.
Every item and skill has its own art, magic weapons glow, and blacksmiths forge gear from monster materials.
Battles show names above each fighter with level and HP below; the map shows faces for you, your companion and your party.
A storybook soundtrack, new sound effects with volume settings, an intro for new heroes and a What's new list.
Friends you've made turn up around the world now and then, and can only join your party when they're nearby.

releases.title: First steps into Fairyland
notes: 14 maps joined by winding roads: Meadowbrook, Rainbow City and Goldburg, plus wild zones from Sunny Meadow to Moonglow.
Random encounters and turn-based battles fought where you stand. Big spells splash onto nearby monsters.
81 monsters across seven elements, with rare colour variants and three bosses.
Capture with Seal Stones and keep up to 5 companions. Your first hatches from the starter egg.
Start as a Novice and join a guild at level 5. Spend skill points to learn and power up skills.
Villagers and adventurers wander and chat. Befriend adventurers and bring two along in your party.
Customise hair, outfit and skin. Armour recolours your outfit and your weapon shows in hand.
Quests, shops, healers, checkpoints, an in-game calendar and a chiptune soundtrack.
